Type: Quirky Event
Key Appearance: Madame Liberty #67, July 1947

Traits:

  • Military Displays d8
  • Summer Heat d8
  • Cheering Crowds d6

GREEN
Minor Twists

  • Parade Marshals: The parade’s marshals move in to separate any violence they see. Roll the environment’s dice, and Defend all targets with the Min die until the next environment turn.
  • Blocked Route: The Bold Bandit drops obstacles in the parade’s path! Create the following challenge: Clear the route.

If the challenge is not resolved by the time the environment changes zones, advance the scene tracker and remove the challenge.
Major Twist

  • It’s Madame Liberty!!: A hero is recognized and swarmed by grateful civilians! Roll the environment dice and Hinder one hero with the Max die.

YELLOW
Minor Twists

  • Seeking the Limelight: A local politician starts trying to make the parade all about them, getting in the way of proper patriotism. Create a d8 “Local Politician” environment lieutenant.
  • Pull Them Onto The Float: Someone gets mistaken for part of the parade and pulled into it! Roll the environment dice. Hinder a Hero with the Mid die and Defend them with the Min die.

Major Twist

  • Twenty-One Gun Salute: The Bold Bandit replaced a squad’s blanks with bullets! Roll the environment dice. Hinder one target with the Max die and Attack another target with the Mid die.

RED
Minor Twists

  • Run Over By A Tank: The parade route isn’t supposed to go through here! Pick a group of targets that are close to each other. Roll the environment dice and Attack all targets with the Max die.
  • La Marseillaise : The crowd begins to sing the national anthem, and everyone is swept with patriotic fervor. Roll the environment dice, and Boost all patriotic targets with the Max die.

Major Twist

  • Overzealous Military Action: A group of French soldiers decide to intervene to save the parade, but they’re liable to cause as much harm as good! Roll the environment dice. Create a number of d10 “Squad of Soldiers” minions equal to the Max die. Half of them will Attack villains, while the other half accidentally Hinder heroes.

In the post-war period, Madame Liberty struggled to find its feet. The character had been designed and defined by her work as an undercover rebel fighting against the Nazi threat, and with the end of the war there was discussion of simply letting the character wrap up and moving on to other things. People were tired of war stories, writers said. They wanted something new and exciting, not to be reminded of the horrors of the past several years.

Vincent Chambers agreed, but Madame Liberty was still one of the three top heroes for Venture Comics, and he refused to toss her aside the way that smaller wartime heroes like the Partisan were being removed. Instead, he created a series of stories about rebuilding in France and western Europe, in which criminals, ex-Nazis, and corrupt businessmen sought to interfere in the country’s reconstruction. With the help of Kid Liberty and Rick Wilson, she did battle with a mostly-forgettable collection of minor supervillains, including a few remnants from the war years. Her stories got increasingly silly, leaning into the new feel of the post-war years, but they were able to generally stay popular.

“The Battle of the Bastille”, published in Madame Liberty #67, was a perfect example of these sorts of tales. As Paris prepared for its annual Bastille Day parade, a villain calling himself the Bold Bandit threatened to destroy the patriotic spirit of France by cancelling the parade! He sent a radio broadcast over the city warning the people not to attend, because France had ‘fallen once, and would fall again’.

Madame Liberty refused to allow this to happen. She and Kid Liberty offered their services to the French government, shadowing the parade and stopping a string of increasingly silly attempts by the Bold Bandit to disrupt the parade, confuse the crowds of people there to watch it, or just run Madame Liberty over with a tank. The Bandit had no powers to speak of; he made use of a string of well-designed traps and gimmicks in his efforts, along with gangs of paid toughs to work his schemes for him.

Ultimately, Madame Liberty tracked down the Bold Bandit, learning that he was a French soldier furious that his nation was claiming to be patriotic after having surrendered to the Nazis during the war. Madame Liberty reminded him of all the French people who had continued to fight under Nazi occupation, and convinced him to turn himself in. The issue ended in a patriotic rendition of La Marseillaise.

If issues like this had continued for much more than two years, Madame Liberty might have ended up as one of the casualties of the end of the Golden Age. Fortunately, the title’s next writer hit on moving the heroine to Berlin as part of her reconstruction efforts, where she came into conflict with Soviet agents led by Iron Will. The Cold War gave Madame Liberty a new place to work her superheroic spycraft, keeping her comic popular through the 1950s and allowing her to secure her place as one of the pinnacle heroes of Venture Comics.

Behind The Scenes:

Back to back Madame Liberty stories, but they definitely show how dramatically her adventures shifted with the end of the war! Two years ago she was battling Nazi mind-control tanks, and now she’s having parade hijinks.

I do love the parade hijinks, though. It’s totally silly for a parade to just keep rolling along during a supervillain action scene, but it’s the right kind of silly. None of the twists actually stop the parade, they just make the situation more chaotic and goofy.

I’m quite proud of both of this week’s environments, and I hope you’ll like them! We’re kicking off the end of our Golden Age tales with…

The Mattson Mire

Mattson Mire600×400 160 KB

Type: Dangerous Location
Key Appearance: Twilight Carnival #60, April 1950
Traits:

  • Strangling Vines d12
  • Life-Draining Mud d10
  • Poisonous Insects d8

GREEN
Minor Twists

  • Mud Men: The mud comes to life! Roll the environment dice and create a number of d8 Mud Men equal to the Min die. If they fail a damage save while at d8 or above, reduce them to d4 instead of destroying them.
  • Poisonous Sting: A cloud of insects descends on a hero. That hero’s player must step down their highest Power or Quality die for the scene. They may restore it with a successful Overcome action.

Major Twist

  • Writhing Roots: The roots of the swamp reach up to devour its victims. Roll the environment dice and Attack all targets not affiliated with the Mire using the Mid die.

YELLOW
Minor Twists

  • Life Unending: The swamp’s power flows into those who seek it. Roll the environment dice and Boost one target affiliated with the Mire using the Max die.
  • Cage of Branches: The swamp reaches out to drag a hero into the muck. Create the following two-step challenge: Break Them Free

Until the challenge is resolved, the hero may not move from their current spot.

Major Twist

  • Drink Deep: The swamp drains the essence from its invaders and gives it to its friends. Roll the environment dice and Attack all targets not affiliated with the Mire using the Mid die. For each target Attacked, Boost one target affiliated with the Mire using the Min die.

RED
Minor Twists

  • Quicksand: The swamp tries to swallow its victims. Roll the environment dice and Hinder all targets not affiliated with the Mire with the Max die.
  • Unearth The Dead: The swamp disgorges its victims. Roll the environment dice and create a number of d8 “Vine-Filled Skeleton” minions equal to the Max die.

Major Twist

  • The Trees Walk: The Mire’s trees wrap around an ally and lash out at their foes. Roll the environment dice and Defend one target with the Max die. Attack all targets not affiliated with the Mire using the Max die.

Note: All environment minions and lieutenants are considered to be affiliated with the Mire. Villains may or may not be depending on the story, and Heroes are never affiliated with the Mire.

While the other superheroes of Venture Comics were struggling, Twilight Carnival thrived by leaning increasingly into horror elements and downplaying the superheroic nature of its protagonist. Under the stewardship of new editor-in-chief Joe Manzetta, the Midnight Rider faced off against the sort of creepy monsters that other comics showed devouring innocents and spreading fear through the world, using her carnival wits and magical tricks to win the day. She often came close to defeat, but never so close as when she investigated the Mattson Mire.

The story began when the Carnival set up in a small New England town. The police came to investigate the disappearance of a young couple, suspecting the carnies of foul play, and in order to clear her friends’ names the Midnight Rider began to investigate. She soon learned that people had been going missing in the region for decades, dating back to a series of mysterious witch trials held in the 1700s. The supposed witchfinder, Mathias Mattson, had in fact been seeking out young women with magical talent, killing them to steal their power for his own; when one of the women cursed him, he was swallowed by the local bog, sinking into the mud. But the stories said that Mattson’s ghost still stalked the swamp, looking for magical women to kill.

The Midnight Rider ventured into the swamp, hoping to free the lost souls contained within. She was shocked to discovered that Mattson was not her foe – it was the Mire itself. The gathered power Mattson had stolen brought the swamp itself to life. It was hungry for magic, infecting the plants, insects, and mud itself with its desire and reaching out to ensnare the unwary. Over time, the Mattson Mire began to send out tendrils of itself, ambushing those with faint magical talent and luring them into the swamp to die.

Armed for a ghost and facing an entire environment, the Midnight Rider fought against the mud men, cursed insects, and grasping vines trying to steal her power. She wasn’t able to save the couple; they were long dead. But she did succeed in sealing the swamp and preventing it from continuing to prey on victims – for now.

The Mire wasn’t intended to be an ongoing threat; the writer of the issue had simply whipped it up for the purposes of the issue. But in 1953, another writer grabbed it for a Cryptic Trails story in which Coven lured Greenheart into the depths of the swamp, planning to use its fell magic to steal her power. Greenheart was able to turn the swamp and the witch against each other, leaving Coven trapped and drained of her magic. When Coven returned, she made an oblique references to having ‘come to terms’ with the Mire.

In the Silver Age, as Coven was reshaped to be a less frightening and more colourful foe to Greenheart, writers wanted her to have a secretive lair that the heroine couldn’t track. A particularly cheeky author gave her Mattson Mire, papering over its more horrific elements to leave it as a creepy living swamp, able to slip through the wilderness and manifest wherever Coven pleased. The Mire served as the first base for the Congress of Deceit, and as Coven grew darker and more frightening the Mire returned to its darker past as well.
As a result, Mattson Mire became a recurring element in several Venture Comics titles over the years. Sometimes a villain would make a deal with the swamp and share power with it, aligning themselves with its dark hunger. Sometimes they would try to steal its might for themselves – both Doctor Freak and Elysium Inc. had major storylines attempting to siphon off the Mire’s power, with heroes caught in the middle as the swamp lashed out at all concerned.

Behind The Scenes:

Evil swamp!

Everyone loves an evil swamp, you know? And it’s a great spot for something that can become part of a lot of different magical forces. It’s an environment, but it’s also potentially the primary enemy, and since it has nebulous relocation powers it can be where you want it to be.

This is a nasty environment, but how nasty mostly depends on whether you’re fighting a villain who’s working alongside it, or a villain who’s trying to steal its power for themselves.
Swamps are magic, everybody knows that

Time to wrap up the Golden Age, and we are…

On The Trail Of A Poisoner

Poisoner600×400 272 KB

Type: Unique
Key Appearance: Company Town #183, June 1953

Traits:

  • The City At Night d10
  • Secrets and Lies d10
  • Violence and Misery d8

Green Zone
Minor Twists

  • A False Lead: Someone was sure they saw a man slip into that alley. Roll the environment dice and Hinder an investigator with the Mid die.
  • Flip An Asset: Someone who helped the poisoner might be convinced to change sides. Create the following challenge: Get Them On Your Side

If the challenge is resolved, create a +2 “Allied Action” bonus that can be used in the next scene.

Major Twist

  • Scuffle In the Streets: A group of would-be muggers try to get the drop on you. They don’t last long, but they get some hits in. Roll the environment dice and Attack all investigators with the Mid die.

YELLOW
Minor Twists

  • Too Late: The poisoner is taking out loose ends, and you’re too late to save them. It’s a grisly sight. Roll the environment dice and Attack an investigator with the Max die, dealing psychic damage.
  • Not Too Late: The poisoner is taking out loose ends, but you’re just in time. Create the following challenge: Save The Poisoning Victim

If the scene tracker advances to the next zone before the challenge is resolved, the victim dies. If the challenge is resolved, create a a +2 “Antidote” bonus that can be used in the next scene.

Major Twist

  • Pursuing Detective: The cops have figured out what’s up, but they’re on the wrong trail – yours! Create a d8 “Dogged Detective” lieutenant. He immediately rolls his status die and Hinders one investigator with the result.

RED
Minor Twists

  • Poison Trap: A gas trap goes off, fouling up the clues and the investigators! Roll the environment dice and Attack one target with the Max die; Hinder all targets in the same zone with the Mid zone.
  • Back Off, Or Else: Digging into the poisonings is drawing all the wrong sorts of attention, and they don’t care if the poisoner is caught or goes free as long as everyone stops making a mess. Create a d10 “Massive Bruiser” lieutenant.

Major Twist

  • Mass Poisoning: The poisoner commits a desperate act of mass poisoning to buy time to escape. Trigger any combination of “Too Late” and “Not Too Late” a total of (H) times. Each hero may only be targeted once by “Too Late”.

By the early 1950s, there were very few superhero comics left at Venture Comics, and most of those were blending themselves with other genres in order to stay popular. Company Town was at the forefront of this shift, blending a growing tendency to draw on noir detective tropes and storylines as the Revenant and a few minor leftover characters struggled against the dominance of Mr. Ferris and his iron-fisted rule.

Company Town #183 was a typical example of the storylines of the title’s last few years, blending mystery action with pulpy superhuman capabilities. The story opened with the mysterious death of a Ferristown reporter, Davis Jamieson in his office. Jamieson had been invented for this issue, but was retroactively revealed to be one of the many sources the Revenant used in his ongoing war against the criminal elements of Ferristown, and the Revenant immediately suspected the involvement of the Company. The police were inclined to view the death as a simple heart attack, but the Revenant knew that the reporter had been working on a big case, investigating corruption, racketeering, and smuggling taking place using the local Grevenworks automobile factory. He investigated the reporter’s home, and discovered that Jamieson had a bottle of brandy that had been laced with a unique poison, one that would leave no trace in the victim’s system aside from a suspicious heart attack.

What followed was a brutal cat and mouse trail as the Revenant and his allies tracked down the poisoner, using the ingredients used to concoct this impossible poison as their lead. As they did so, however, their target was also hard at work taking out anyone with information about the factory and its corruption. Workers who had seen mysterious things, criminals who had taken part in the smuggling, and officials who had accepted anonymous bribes were all targets, and the Revenant raced through town to identify the next victims and save them. Some of them he was able to reach just in time; others were already dead when he arrived, poisoned through air vents, darts, and drinks. Each poison was different, created using new formulas and deployment methods, but every one led to a signature heart attack.

Despite the poisoner’s best efforts, the Revenant was able to determine who was gathering the ingredients – the secretary to Thomas Manford, one of the night shift foremen at the factory. Racing against time, the Revenant saved the secretary from being Manford’s next victim, and learned from her that Manford was actually a brilliant chemist whose inventions had gone unnoticed by his peers, forcing him to take a factory job to make ends meet. Filled with bitterness at the world, Manford became determined to take Grevenworks down, and to make the living that he felt that he was owed.

With his chemical genius, Manford had begun faking damage to factory goods, inflicting seeming structural damage that could be easily wiped away with the right solvent. Using a few of his workers as accomplices, he had been hiring cheap workers as scapegoats, blaming them for his floor’s above-average damage levels, and then selling the pieces on the black market. Grevenworks was being hit coming and going, with their costs rising rapidly and their sales dropping as the market was flooded with equally-effective but much less expensive goods, and Manford was making the cash he needed to retire to France.

Of course, the scheme couldn’t last. The one hole in the plan was that all of the workers had to run through Manford’s section, and when Jamieson began sniffing around to find the source of the black market goods and the reason for the rapidly-dropping share price of Grevenworks, Manford realized that there were loose ends everywhere connecting him back to the scheme. Jamieson had suspected that the plot was one of Ferris’s attempts to snuff out a competitor; because of that, he hadn’t realized that Manford was his target, and had allowed the poisoner into his home for an interview. But Manford knew that what Jamieson could uncover, others could as well. He’d started covering his tracks, but he was too late.

The Revenant confronted Manford in his office, laying out the plot and demanding that the criminal turn himself in. Instead, Manford pricked the Revenant with a poisoned pin, then dragged his corpse to the rooftop with the goal of framing him as the killer. The Revenant revived, of course, standing from behind Manford and hissing his name, and the terrified criminal leaped from the roof to his death. It was a grim conclusion to a grim story – perfectly in theme for the Revenant’s final outings, but also a key part of the reason that he wasn’t retooled following the implementation of the Comics Code.

Behind The Scenes:

I wanted to slip something challenging into the mix for the Golden Age, and this seemed like the right time for it; not a lot of things with long-term effect were happening in the early 50s. Instead, we get an investigation playing out as an action scene.

There are a lot of different ways to handle investigations in Sentinel Comics, none of them particularly canonical. This felt like a good chance to try something very different.

It’s also a bit longer than usual! Because of the layout issues, I need to have an extra page at the end of each age. In the past, I used a dangling lieutenant to solve that layout problem, but I don’t have anything like that for environments, so the last environment of each age needs to have a two-page writeup. Gave us some time to delve into the Mysterious Manford, who is not ever going to appear again.

  • Gawking Bystanders d8

Minor Twists

  • Squad Backup: A young beat cop recognizes the heroes and quickly moves to support them. Roll the environment dice and Boost one hero with the Mid die.

Over the course of the 1950s, Flatfoot settled into his role as a ‘special deputy’ of the Ferrisville Police Department. Despite being a problem initially, the feud between Company Town and Flatfoot Adventures had proven to be the character’s salvation; by the time the Comics Code came into effect in 1954, Flatfoot had already almost completely abandoned any stories about corrupt officers or politicians, letting those writers work on the Revenant while Flatfoot dealt with more colourful opposition. As a result, the Silver Age version of the character was a member of a thriving and honest police force. The officers were sometimes too zealous, and there were stories where some beat cop or detective clashed with Flatfoot over their belief that he was no more than a mobile tool that shouldn’t be operating unsupervised, but they always ended with Flatfoot bringing them around to his point of view.

Operating out of the FPD’s Central Precinct building, Flatfoot reported directly to Police Commissioner Whitby, and largely had complete autonomy for patrols and investigations, focusing on the field of super-crime and organized criminal activity. Whitby would give Flatfoot tips when reports of super-powered criminals came in, and he would request Flatfoot’s support for major crime busts and make sure that the superhero’s investigations didn’t run afoul of active police investigations, but for most of the 1950s the only part of the Central Precinct that writers bothered to show was Whitby’s office. Various individual police officers came and went, none of them making much of an impact; Flatfoot’s civilian allies such as Colin Harper were more interesting to writers, and there wasn’t much time for socializing when there was crime afoot!

Flatfoot #196 was the first time the precinct served as the focus for a story, rather than just a backdrop. In the previous issue, Flatfoot had rounded up Wise Guy’s gang of mooks. The smart-dressed supervillain knew he couldn’t tangle with Flatfoot directly, but he had a line on just the tough to help him out: he hired the Retriever to break into Ferrisville’s Central Precinct while Wise Guy’s mooks were being processed, in order to free them and bring them back to Wise Guy. While the Retriever burst in the front, the villain slipped in the back, trusting that either Flatfoot would be busy stopping the giant robot, or it would meet with him at the cells and they could leave together.

The resulting chaos led to nearly a full issue of Flatfoot dealing with one problem after another. First he wrestled with the Retriever in the front offices of the building, mistakenly thinking the Retriever was here to kidnap Chief Whitby after it deliberately feinted towards him. He was able to drive the robot off, but the chaos allowed criminals to escape into the streets, forcing Flatfoot to go after them as the police tried to restore order in their own offices. Flatfoot was able to track down and re-arrest each group of villains, ending with Wise Guy himself – the gangster and his mooks were in the middle of celebrating their escape when Flatfoot burst through the door and challenged them once again. With the Retriever having completed its mission successfully and departed, Wise Guy was no match for Flatfoot, and he ended up cooling his heels in a patched-up jail cell alongside his gang.

This was the first time that the FPD was attacked, but it wouldn’t be the last. Over the course of the Silver Age the precinct would be targeted a half-dozen times, and most major Flatfoot adaptations would include a scene of a villain striking at the precinct with the goal of catching Flatfoot off guard or denying him his support. The string of attacks would be one of the reasons Flatfoot would give after his supposed death for why he needed to stay undercover.

Behind The Scenes:

This is sort of halfway between a heroic location and a standard one, but I decided to lean standard because even though Flatfoot kind of operates out of here it’s got a lot of elements that are hostile - escaping criminals, chaotic crowds, that sort of thing.

I wanted to touch on Silver Age Flatfoot’s supporters, and since this is the period in which the Ferrisville police are trustworthy it made sense to create a police commissioner for him. From there I pulled together a quick story, tossed in another villain name that I don’t have a lot of details about but I love the name, and there we go! Wise Guy will eventually get a writeup but I’m pretty sure he’s just a lieutenant who’s an example of the “guy with gang” level of villains that are a lot of Flatfoot’s second-tier opponents.

The Grovedale Museum of Culture had the unique distinction of being the first location present in a Skybreaker adventure, serving as the opening for Venture into the Unknown #2 and the first appearance of the Celtic hero. While it had very little focus time in that issue, the fact that Rhonda Randall worked at the museum, and got Cooper his first job there as a fellow historian, meant that for much of the Silver Age it served as a location for social scenes, a source of secondary characters, and an after-hours base of operations for Skybreaker. In the early issues, Skybreaker slept in the back of the museum, often avoiding the well-meaning but ancient security guard that patrolled the place, and used its resources in the rare cases when he needed to examine clues to track down a super-criminal. Once Rhonda finally convinced him to get an apartment, the museum remained a common meeting ground.

Starting in Skybreaker Stories #12, the Museum also became an occasional battleground. In his third appearance, the Locksmith decided that while he couldn’t track down Skybreaker, he could trace his steps back to where he had first appeared. The devious villain followed the trail of the shipments that had brought the spear his mysterious employer demanded to the museum, and determined that more such artifacts might be hidden in the collection. Deciding to leave the Spear of Assal for the time being, he raided the museum while no one should be around, determined to get his hands on other mystical artifacts.

Of course, someone was around. Cooper and Rhonda were in the museum lab, Rhonda having stayed late to discuss Cooper’s latest escapades as Skybreaker and remind him that he needed to be careful not to have his secret identity found out. As the criminals overran the museum, the two of them were promptly captured, leaving Cooper with a dilemma – reveal his power and threaten his secret, or leave Rhonda in danger and the artifacts under threat?

Rhonda solved the problem for him, deliberately creating a distraction so that Cooper could ‘run for help’. The hero slipped into the darkness of the museum, drawing his spear and transforming into Skybreaker, as Rhonda was captured by the Locksmith’s men. The Locksmith told Rhond that he admired her smarts, but she had just gone from captive to hostage. He kept her close at hand as he grabbed artifacts, uncovering an ancient bracelet that could summon rains and using it to flood out the street outside and slow the police from arriving!

With Rhonda and the museum both in danger, Skybreaker was forced to use subtlety for the first time since his awakening. He carefully took down each goon in turn, using the museum’s security systems and Wilbur’s assistance, before finally allowing the Locksmith to leave the building with Rhonda and his acquired goods before confronting him outside. Rhonda grabbed the bracelet off the Locksmith’s hands, and Skybreaker took him down, sending him to jail for the first time (but far from the last).

The Grovedale Museum of Culture remained a constant in Skybreaker’s stories from his first appearance all the way through to the Diamond Age. Over the course of their tenure, Cooper Cullen and Rhonda Randall were both employees at the museum, with Rhonda working her way up the ranks from historian to assistant curator to curator by the Iron Age, before having to step back during her early years as Solace. Both heroes continued to work for the museum part-time, but their increasingly complicated schedules forced them to pull back from what had been their effective headquarters; by the Diamond Age, the museum was mostly used as a backdrop for adventures instead of a common meeting ground.

Behind The Scenes:

Our first heroic base of operations. The Grovedale Museum of Culture is generally on the side of the heroes; the only real danger is that all of the stuff in there is going to get broken. I also get to write up Wilbur, who was probably the source of a lot of Silver Age goofs, then returned in the Bronze Age as a semi-retired museum attendee. I think that he’s too popular to lose, so he gets rewound back to his initial age as part of Cooper’s wishcrafted world in the Iron Age. There is almost certainly a 90+ year old Wilbur occasionally showing up in Starshadow.

This is also our first formal Locksmith story. I have a feel for Locksmith’s character, which is ironic because I do not have the faintest clue what his powers are. He definitely has powers, he’s not just a guy with gadgets, and they’re probably in some way related to doing crimes, but no idea what. I don’t think he literally just opens locks, he’s not Skeleton Key. Something more vaguely connected to the theme of “being the guy you hire to break something open for you”.

And finally, while writing up the background for this one, I have discovered that in Volume 1 and Volume 4 of Venture Comics, Rhonda is “Rhonda Randall”. In Volume 2, she is “Rhonda Rhodes”. In Volume 3, she is both “Rhonda Randall” and “Rhonda Rhodes”. So I’m going to have to edit all of that. She is meant to be Rhonda Randall.

Launched in 1961, the bi-monthly Champions of Truth had two major objectives. The first of these was to draw the attention of readers of Venture’s established heroes, Flatfoot and Madame Liberty, to the newly-established or returned stalwarts of the Venture line. The second was to give space for big action scenes and plots that were too complex for one hero to solve. This meant that early Champions of Truth stories especially didn’t spend a lot of time on delving deep into the characterization and supporting casts of the heroes; they had their own titles for that. Instead, that space was given to setting up broad villainous plots before the Champions arrived to stop them.

Because of this, many early Champions of Truth stories featured either a traditional opponent of one of the team’s five members coming up with a particularly devastating plot, as with Doctor Freak in Champions of Truth #1, or two or more villains joining forces to unleash a combined scheme that threatened a city, nation, or the planet. “Toil and Trouble”, the fourth issue of Champions of Truth, was one of the latter sort of story. The Greenheart villain Coven had made a few appearances by this point, but while she had some support she wasn’t taken particularly seriously by readers. To buff up her reputation, and to have some fun, writer Alan Victor decided to combine her with the much more popular Madame Liberty foes the Dread Dynasty, taking on a goofy rendition of Macbeth in which the Dauphin de Sabre sought to overthrow the Royal Family of England and take the throne of the United Kingdom.

The story opened with Coven approaching de Sabre as he and his retainers plotted their next scheme to claim the throne of France. She pointed out the historical ties between the two nations, and prophesized that she saw Dauphin in the Tower of London, wearing the Crown Jewels of England. Her honeyed words tempted the Dauphin and his followers, and they agreed to lauch their assault, holding all of London hostage to claim the crown! Coven called up a massive storm, filled with dark spirits of wind and thunder, and used her magic to reinforce the Dynasty and curse their foes as they rampaged through the streets with the support of the Dauphin’s supporters, the Footmen.

Through Wonderer’s magic, the Champions of Truth responded immediately, taking to the streets to slow the Dynasty down. Madame Liberty and Skybreaker fought against the Dauphin as Flatfoot and Wonderer saved civilians and battled minor members of the Dynasty; Greenheart used her connection to the Green to track down Coven and confront her, breaking her spells and shattering the storm over London. Coven’s prophecy came true; the Dauphin entered the Tower and placed the Crown on his head. But immediately afterwards, he discovered that Madame Liberty had already switched out the jewels, and he was wearing a fake! With no cultural artifacts to use as a shield and no magic coming to save him, he was quickly defeated. Coven escaped into the night, cursing the Champions as the Dread Dynasty was rounded up.

“Toil and Trouble” was a huge success, and Greenheart’s prominence in it began to set the stage for her finally getting her own comic in 1963. The storyline also paved the way for the formation of the Congress of Deceit at the end of the year; while the Dread Dynasty was considered to be too high-profile to take part as Madame Liberty’s nemesis, Coven’s successful showing in this story allowed Victor to slip her in, saving the character from obscurity.

Behind The Scenes:

This started as an excuse to do something fun with the Dread Dynasty and it turned into an excuse to make a lot of Macbeth quotes.

I like this story as an example of the sort of thing that Champions of Truth is up to in the early sixties - just giving big stompy action scenes for a rotating array of Champions villains, growing into the launch of the Congress of Deceit in December. There aren’t a lot of stories for this title early on, since it’s only every other month, but I can imagine a handful of other options for what they’re up to. I expect there are at least three of these double team-ups out of the four issues from #2 through #5. Not sure who, precisely. One of them is probably a Mary Molotov/Steeldriver team-up that gets really out of hand.

The Wonderer’s early stories tended to be lower-stakes, especially compared to many of his contemporaries. His stories largely alternated between two styles – manifesting to ordinary people to offer them a wish, leading to comic upsets and a lesson learned, or traveling with his young ward Khalil and running into a petty or whimsical supervillain who needed to be stopped.

Wondrous Adventures #7 was one of the latter stories. When Khalil wished to be invited to a ‘real, high society party’, the Wonderer used his magic to transform the pair of them into visiting Arab nobility, securing an invitation to a grand party being thrown by the richest people in Ferrisville (including Hank Ferris Jr., included as a fake-out to suggest he would be the villain of the issue before almost immediately declaring the event a ‘bore’ and departing.) Khalil was having a wonderful time chatting with the children of the wealthy aristocrats as Barquan easily chatted with the adults and considered which one he might offer a wish to.

Before the Wonderer could make his choice, however, one of the partygoers discovered a golden trophy sitting on the central table, labeled “To The Fairest”. Everyone agreed that it was a roaring joke, a take on the old Greek myth. Then they started jokingly arguing over who would qualify, just as if the myth was taking place.

Then the jokes turned sour. Factions formed. The most successful members of Ferristown society began eyeing each other suspiciously, and when socialite Richard Mills suddenly pushed his fiancée out of the way to grab the Trophy, all hell broke loose. The more someone wanted the Trophy, the stronger they became, even able to shrug off the Wonderer’s magic.

The Wonderer had sensed the flow of magic in the area, and he set to work trying to keep all of the socialites from hurting each other while he simultaneously tried to unweave the powerful magic causing everyone to believe themselves the rightful owner of the Trophy, and to find the villain responsible. Over the course of the issue, he managed to keep the various fights and arguments at a comical level, narrowly avoiding a few fatalities. He was aided by Gus Fairbanks, an easy-going man who seemed completely untouched by the situation, cheerfully playing piano while everyone around him raged.

It was Gus’s detachment that made Wonderer realize that the Trophy wasn’t drawing on greed or vanity, but on insecurity. He was the only partygoer who wasn’t worried about his social standing, and thus didn’t care one whit about the trophy. With that key, the Wonderer and Khalil were able to play keep-away with the Trophy, letting Wonderer undo its magic while Khalil rallied the children to the ‘game’ of frustrating their parents, and calm the situation down.

Once the situation was resolved, the Wonderer unmasked Giselle, one of the women who’d been egging on the situation, as the supervillain the Minx. The Minx had the mystical power to bring objects and beings from fables to life, creating chaos and mischief. She pouted about being caught, but admitted that the Wonderer had won – this time! She vanished before he could magically bring her to justice, but he consoled himself with the knowledge that her plot had been ruined – and Khalil had had a wonderful afternoon.

Behind The Scenes:

I had originally planned for these environments to almost exclusively include issues about either one-shot villains or villains we already know about. I’ve mostly succeeded, but I liked the idea of a quirky Wondrous Adventures event and Avarice just did not fit, so we get a new second-tier Wonderer villain. I suspect the Minx is a dedicated C-Lister, who never has a really big defining storyline but has an entertaining enough gimmick as a low-tier reality shaper that people just kind of toss her in when they want to goof around with a classic myth or fable without creating new Venture Comics deep lore. I might give her a full write-up some day, we’ll see.

For the story itself, it’s just goofy. It’s a hot potato that takes time to unspool, and people are constantly trying to grab it from you. The best bet is for one hero to grab it and pass it to a second hero before they get obsessed, and then that hero works on the main challenge, and then a bad guy grabs it and you have to repeat the process.

The early 1960s were largely an excuse for Neutrino to fly to whatever strange and mysterious space things his writers could imagine, do some super-heroing there, and then fly away. No one particularly cared about making them scientifically accurate and most of them never appeared again, but occasionally something would pop up that was strange enough that it would leave a mark on the pages of Venture Comics.

The Zlytaran Nexus was such a place. It first appeared in a simple story in 1961, in which it was not particularly interrogated or discussed. It was simply a mine where ‘Time was mined’, with a vague implication that this was a fuel used by interstellar travel. Neutrino saved the miners from a space beast that devoured Time to grow incredibly quickly, and moved on.

In Celestial Travels #298 and #299, though, the Nexus would become a much bigger part of Neutrino’s story. The Interstellar Trading Guild had just made overtures to the Nexus and its workers, but as they sought to bring it into the fold, the region was attacked by Subjugator. She was in search of the powerful time crystals that formed in the nebula’s unusual radiations, and which had the power to speed up or slow down the flow of time. Rumours said that particularly pure crystals could allow for actual time travel, and Subjugator intended to travel back in time and steal rare artifacts before they became rare, so that she wouldn’t have to deal with any of the security that now surrounded them.

Neutrino responded to a distress call from his reluctant ally Lieutenant Heerah, using the ITG’s gates to quickly skip back to the Nexus. After a brief dogfight that saw the Aurora Borealis nearly destroyed, he slipped into the mines themselves, tracking down Heerah and saving her from the Starbooters before challenging Subjugator directly. Her reckless operation was threatening to unleash the temporal energies of the nebula, dooming everyone present, and Neutrino tried and failed to convince her that her goal was just too dangerous.

In the ensuing fight, the Aurora Borealis was destroyed – but at the start of Celestial Travels #299 a stray time eddy *un-*destroyed it, allowing Neutrino to pursue Subjugator as she navigated the Nexus towards the pure time crystals that she had discovered. Neutrino defeated Subjugator and freed the Nexus, but in the battle his own radioactive energies merged with the energies of the Nexus, leading him to spend Celestial Travels #300 hopping through his own timeline, attempting to change history to prevent himself from leaving Earth and ultimately only managing to create the conditions that had allowed him to survive his transformation.

The Zlytaran Nexus remained a popular part of Venture’s galactic network, however. Zlytaran crystals could be used as a shorthand to empower various science fiction technologies, allowing for rapid cloning devices, specialized healing chambers, and stasis fields that could be deployed by individual supervillains but whose extremely rare power source kept them from being something that had to be reckoned with as a common part of galactic life. Over the years the Nexus would be attacked by the Uranians, the Kliz’Exth, and various smaller groups, but without the generations of knowledge that the local miners had developed to manage and live in harmony with the local temporal landscape, none of them were able to hold it for long.

Behind The Scenes:

Time Crystals!

It’s just the sort of absolutely silly science fantasy nonsense that you got in Silver Age comics, it has staying power to be useful for decades to come, it gives me both a new material and a new location, everything about this place is perfect.

I wasn’t sure if I was going to give Celestial Travels a weird place or a heroic ITG base, but the randomizers lined up nicely for the former and here we are! Maybe not as weird as the next environment I’m going to build, but plenty weird enough!

In Vanguards! #71, Realm of the Riddlemaster, an experiment with Doctor Cosmos’ orb went awry, sending the Vanguards careening into a pocket dimension. In the strangely-patterned world they met a strange cat-like alien that called itself the Riddlemaster. Declaring that it hadn’t seen travellers in over a millenium, the creature immediately asked to play with them, promising to help the Vanguards leave if they could solve its games. Captain Bolt refused, but Mr. Infinity felt sorry for the lonely person, and told them that he’d be happy to play for a bit.

The Riddlemaster immediately perked up and began creating obstacles and puzzles for Mr. Infinity. It quickly became obvious that the entire fabric of the dimension was theirs to command, able to create illusions of life and even rewrite the Vanguards’ powers and abilities on a whim. After a series of nearly fatal challenges, with the Riddlemaster lending a hand when they seemed about to lose but adding more challenges every time the heroes seemed about to win, the Vanguards were able to more or less solve its riddles. True to their word, the Riddlemaster opened a portal for the team to leave, telling the group that they hadn’t had that much fun in eons. They apologized for causing trouble, admitting that knew that when the game was done they would be alone again. Impulsively, seeing the Riddlemaster looking forlorn as the group was leaving, Mr. Infinity turned back and told them that the Vanguards would be their friends, and that they would visit again some day. Captain Bolt dourly predicted that would mean trouble down the line, but he couldn’t fault Reggie for his compassion.

The Riddlemaster wasn’t meant to be more than one of the random strange things that the Vanguards encountered, but fate had other ideas. One month after “Realm of the Riddlemaster”, Sentinel Comics unveiled a multi-issue event featuring their own cosmic imp, Wager Master. Seeing the popularity of the blue chaos god, Joe Manzetta went to Kit Granville and demanded more stories for Venture’s own trickster. Granville shrugged and tossed a goofy Riddlemaster story into the mix early in 1965, in which the imp appeared in the middle of a battle between the Vanguards and the Malefactors to ‘cheer my favourite heroes on’, sowing chaos and confusion.

From then on, the Riddlemaster would appear randomly to play with their friends, with an unclear grasp on the line between ‘goofy fun’ and ‘deadly force’ combined with an ever-shifting series of rules about how they could interact with the universe. Sometimes they would help save the day, other times they would make the situation much worse, but they always meant well. Later stories would codify that the Riddlemaster was bound by the same rules that affected gods such as Urak or the Empress of Ash, and had been allowed into Earth’s dimension by Mr. Infinity’s declaration of friendship. If they stayed for too long, they would begin to break down existence and absorb it into their own lonely realm, which was why their visits were so short.

When Doctor Cosmos left the Vanguards to travel with the Celestial Travellers, the Riddlemaster followed her, becoming a recurring character in Celestial Travels while also popping in to Earth to offer new challenges to the Vanguards. Both teams were fond of but frustrated by the godling, and did their best to guide it to better life choices while surviving the nonsense it threw their way. This helped it to stay relevant while the Vanguards were out of the picture in the 1990s, and they remained a minor fan favorite through to the present.

In the early years of the Riddlemaster’s appearances, it would pop up as a man, woman, both, or neither according to its whim; the 2010s codified them as a being that had been non-binary even before developing infinite cosmic power, and who used that power to maintain whatever gender was most comfortable in the moment.

Behind The Scenes:

Back to Hero Forge for a bit, that’s nice.

The Riddlemaster was of course first mentioned back in Deep Cuts as the originator of the Cosmic Mr. Infinity variant. At the time, I mentioned they’d be getting more information, and here they are! As a cosmic imp who is more careless than malicious, the Riddlemaster doesn’t really make sense as a villain, but they’re a great environment. You can also mix and match some of their twists with another environment if they’re getting involved somewhere else.

I do have more Riddlemaster stuff to write up one day, but this is as much as I could fit in this section of the story. They’re definitely one of those folks that gets a few contradictory backstories and eventually one of them sticks; I like the idea that as the 70s go on and people start more directly codifying the idea of ancient godlike beings who can dissolve worlds through their presence, and thus are prevented from travelling between dimensions unless certain conditions are met, the Riddlemaster gets elevated to joining Urak, Balor, Amorta and the Sovereign - but much less malicious, which means that their ability to absorb worlds is actually a huge problem for them that they try to avoid.

In the real world, the Riddlemaster is a tiny bit personal because they’re based on an in-joke between me and my spouse that kind of got out of hand. Spouse had final say on the look, and gave it two thumbs up.

As Liberty’s Dream picked up steam, it often delved into politics in ways that skirted the lines of what was allowable under the Comics Code, with frequent complaints about how close many of Reverie’s opponents were coming to representing law enforcement or business leaders. After the third such complaint, Joe Manzetta went to the title’s author, Quentin Jones, and all but begged him to include a storyline in which Reverie fought against Communists, just to create the impression that the publication cared. With a practiced innocent expression that Manzetta had learned to recognize as trouble, Jefferson agreed. He returned to his office, sat down with his artistic partner Charlie Lake, and laid out his plans for the Red Scare.

Liberty’s Dream #24 thus opened up with Reverie getting wind of strange activities taking place in a run-down part of Havenwood. Small-time crooks were suddenly spouting Soviet propaganda, having run-ins with the cops, and whipping up discontent with the state of the neighborhood into a frenzy. Whispers said that the mastermind of the affair was the Red Scare, a supervillain with the power to unlock the dreams in people’s hearts and bring them to life – so long as they committed themselves to the Cause.

It all sounded very suspicious to Reverie, and more than a little magical. At the very least, she expected that these ‘Communists’ were just looking for meat to turn against America, leaving them high and dry when the bill came due. She arrived in Havenwood looking for trouble, and it didn’t take long for her to find it. There was Communist propaganda everywhere, most of it poorly written and even more poorly articulated, promising free money, an end to long working days, no more bosses breathing down your necks.

But Reverie couldn’t find any trace of magic in the situation. She was just starting to wonder if she was dealing with an offshoot of a Soviet mind-controller like Iron Will, who she had previously fought alongside the Champions of Truth, when the Red Scare announced a major speech that would direct his ‘followers’ to ‘overthrow the Capitalist Regime’. Confused and curious crowds, suspicious police officers, and federal agents began to gather, ready for trouble, and Reverie moved in to make sure that things didn’t get out of hand.

Which they did. Agents of the Red Scare exploded out of the crowd, attacking police officers and civilians alike as bombs went off in local storefronts. Reverie used her powers to save people and stop the provocateurs, only to discover that they were just more small-time crooks in stolen gear. She confronted the Red Scare, only to discover that he was another small-time crook who had been paid a few hundred dollars to put on the suit, and the penny dropped.

Using her powers to race through the Underhill, Reverie emerged at the farthest point across town from the gathering – the Garamond Technological Research Center. There, she was able to ambush the true mastermind behind the Red Scare – the Red Herring! The capering villain had deliberately created a false Communist menace to distract the defenders of the city from his true target, grabbing more high-powered technology for his mercenary schemes. Reverie was able to stop the Herring’s robbery, but he escaped before she could corner him, promising with a glint in his eye that the two would meet again.

Jones deliberately held back the script until it was too late to change it. Manzetta was predictably furious, but after a roaring fight that was audible across the bullpen he reluctantly allowed it. The argument ended up being one of the factors that led to Jones leaving Venture Comics in 1966, preferring to make comics without an editor breathing down his neck.

Behind The Scenes:

This was one of those things that sort of reverse-engineered itself.

I wanted a Red Herring story. I had been plotting out other possible Soviet supervillains to fight Madame Liberty and a villain called “The Red Scare” popped into my mind, but it was pretty close to the Red Herring. And then I thought, “I absolutely bet he would make that a fake villain as a bit” and then here we are.

I wasn’t sure who to give it to originally; I was back and forth between this being a Liberty’s Dream story and a Covert Tactics one, and finally ended up flipping a coin. I like it as a “no, really, anyone can end up facing the Red Herring” thing.

After returning to Europe from her brief arc in Vietnam, the writers of Madame Liberty quickly made sure to focus on traditional superheroic adventures defending European freedom from dangerous foreign powers and criminal superheroes. In November 1965, the team introduced a new supporting character for the title, Pierre Levesque. Levesque was a foppish but brilliant inventor whose father had founded a major industrial company with reconstruction money following the end of World War II; Pierre had inherited the company and largely left it to run itself while siphoning off funds for his personal projects. Fortunately for the company, his personal projects were wildly successfully, and the Levesque Advanced Science and Technology Centre (commonly called LAST) was soon the primary destination for European super-science.

Pierre was first introduced when Iron Will attempted to kidnap and brainwash him during a routine visit to oversee investments in West Berlin; Madame Liberty saved him, and out of gratitude he began supplying her with his latest gadgets for her adventures, providing her with a supersonic one-person jet and various cutting-edge tools that he wrote off as prototype experiments. Marianne actually liked the man, and for a few months there was a subplot about Rick Wilson being annoyed by Pierre’s flirtations, but the pair didn’t go anywhere, and in *Madame Liberty #*293, in May 1966, Pierre was over the moon about his new girlfriend Mina, who he introduced to Marianne and Rick with great fanfare.

Mina made a couple of appearances over the next several months, and it was obvious from the first that she was up to something, but it wasn’t until Madame Liberty #298 that the heroine discovered her secret – she was, in fact, Grand Duchess Gloria Mantalos, the White Mantis, in disguise! She had been secretly dating Pierre in order to steal his designs and technology, and was planning a raid on his facility to acquire everything that LAST had produced.

In Madame Liberty #299, Madame Liberty and Rick Wilson went to LAST to warn Pierre and confront White Mantis, only to discover that she had tricked the staff into thinking that they were imposters and turned the facility against them! The duo had to fight their way through the facility as White Mantis’s raid began, convincing security to change sides and finally saving Pierre from kidnapping by the skin of their teeth. Madame Liberty followed White Mantis back to Granlavia for a major confrontation, which took place in the following issue, leaving Pierre to rebuild his lab.

While that was the first major breach of LAST, the facility would continue to appear over the coming decades, with Pierre a common supporting character who found himself in trouble with an array of villains. During the AEGIS era, LAST was briefly a major AEGIS supplier before Covert Tactics was able to present evidence of the agency’s duplicity to Pierre and convince him to sever his contracts, and he continued to provide technology to a few of his favourite superhero teams without the knowledge or approval of Levesque Industries’ Board of Directions. Pierre eventually married another minor Covert Tactics supporting character, Janie McClinnon, in the late 1990s, and by the Diamond Age was semi-retired and allowing his daughter Cybele to handle the family business while he tinkered in his lab and enjoyed long vacations with his wife.

Behind The Scenes:

We’ve had a lot of tech supervillains, but not a lot of tech companies, so I thought I would use Madame Liberty to introduce a European one and flesh out a few minor characters at the same time. It’s a fun White Mantis plot, a lab whose inventor is neither a superhero nor a supervillain but just an absent-minded professor, and some fun long-term development. Just don’t get the scientists killed!

And speaking of vacations! I am off next week for my spouse’s birthday, so this thread will be a bit quiet. I’ll be back on the 27th, so feel free to keep the chatter going and guess about what environments might be coming up.

Major Silver Age heroes in Venture Comics had highly variable secret identities, ranging from Skybreaker’s true identity only being known to Rhonda Randall all the way to Flatfoot simply existing as a public hero. Greenheart was one of the more secretive characters, theoretically disguised as Italian exchange student Val Turner at Grovedale College, but over the course of the sixties her secret identity was revealed to a growing number of people, mostly because she was a terrible liar. “Val awkwards fails to hide her identity from various supporting cast members who in turn pretend that they don’t know that she’s a superhero” became a running joke in Into The Green, with a new person learning Greenheart’s secret identity every three or four issues.

Val and Ginnie’s group of friends, all of whom had learned the hero’s identity and gamely pretended that they hadn’t, tended to hang out at a diner on the edge of campus called Cliff’s. The eponymous owner and chef of the diner was never drawn, hanging out in the kitchen and yelling out orders; Ginnie worked at the diner as a waitress, and Val enjoyed exploring the mysterious modern foods that the diner had on offer.

The illusion that her secret identity was secure was broken in Into the Green #50, when Dr. Freak attacked Grovedale with his latest army of monstrous minions, hoping to force Greenheart out of hiding and learn how her powers operated. Freak had no idea who Greenheart really was, and indeed hadn’t considered that she might have a secret identity at all; he believed that she lived in the wilderness and emerged to fight crime. But what he did have was a map of locations that she tended to appear from, and he send squads of twisted animals to each of those locations to flush the hero out of hiding. When the attack began, Val was at the diner with Ginnie and her friends, and panicked as she tried to fight the creatures while covering up her capabilities. Aspen bounded in from the forest to help, but the enemies were everywhere and the gathered students weren’t up to the task of protecting themselves.

After a couple pages of awkward slapstick comedy in which Val put herself in harm’s way to protect everyone without revealing herself, Cliff yelled out from the kitchen for Val to ‘do her plant thing before we’re all et up!’ Realizing that her identity was busted, and with lives on the line, Val revealed herself as Greenheart and crushed the monsters, before racing out to fight them across the city.

In the aftermath, Val returned to Cliff’s to shamefacedly apologize for lying to her friends, only to find them gathered around and ready to shamefacedly apologize for lying to her. They’d known that her secret was important to her, and had been trying to let her live a normal life as much as possible, but that had just caused her to get hurt trying to protect them and keep her secret. Even Cliff admitted (from the kitchen) that he’d seen Val go into the bathroom and then emerge from the alley as Greenheart three different times.

The incident became a running gag both within the pages of Into the Green and in the broader readership, with Val’s not-so-secret identity very slowly eroding over the course of the 1970s before imploding completely in the Iron Age. But Cliff’s stayed a gathering place for her and the friends who were willing to treat her as just a person, not a symbol, and while Cliff grumbled sometimes about the small-time villains that crashed the place, he also made sure to always have a piece of pie at hand for his favourite superhero.

Behind The Scenes:

I got halfway through writing this up as a college bar and then I remembered that heroes weren’t allowed to drink alcohol before 1971 so that was right out. So we get a diner instead!

Greenheart’s secret identity is something that I’ve been musing over for a while; I had indicated in her Silver Age writeup that she had one, but by the Iron Age she’s been written as just being Valeria Tertia and having no real civilian life to speak of. So I thought I would thread the needle and explain why her secret identity faded away.

I think that Ginnie Turner and the college kids never fully vanish from Greenheart stories, but the more that her storylines focus on True Rome stuff the less present they are. Cliff’s definitely sticks around and makes cameos in other Grovedale heroes’ stories, because it’s a fun little easter egg.

FrivYeti:

I got halfway through writing this up as a college bar and then I remembered that heroes weren’t allowed to drink alcohol before 1971 so that was right out.

Well, sort of. That was pure Comics Code self-censorship, and sure as heck didn’t apply before 1954. There were quite a few instances of heroic (and villainous) tippling in the 1940s and early 50s, and not just in capes books. Any proper cowboy who couldn’t hold his liquor in those days was not going to go very far, and racket-busting mystery men throughout the 30s were still dealing with the legacy of former bootleggers turned generalist crime bosses.

1967 though, yeah, wrong time period for hanging out in a hooch joint for mainstream publishers anyway. Just a little too early.
